# Hati walks into a space, astronomy & celestial science firm

Somewhere right now, in a space, astronomy & celestial science office, someone is doing exactly what the myths describe — and has never heard of **Hati**. This file is the introduction.

## Before the Office, the Story

**The Pair Before Heaven.** The name's one poetic attestation comes in Óðinn's great catalogue of the cosmos in Grímnismál, where the disguised god enumerates the heavens for the torture-bound Geirrøðr: 'Skǫll is the name of the wolf who follows the bright-faced god to the sheltering wood; but the other is Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, who runs before the bright bride of heaven. ' The bright bride of heaven is the sun; the wolf who runs before her is on the heels of the moon, which travels ahead of her.  In four lines the Edda converts the machinery of the sky into a hunt: what astronomy calls a course, the poem calls a chase.

**Skǫll After the Sun, Hati After the Moon.** Snorri systematizes the verse.  When Gangleri asks why the sun hurries so — 'she speeds as if she were afraid' — High One answers that she has good cause: 'the one who seeks her is right behind her, and she has no other way out than to run. ' Two wolves do the work of the heavens: Skǫll chases the sun and will catch her, and 'the other wolf is called Hati Hróðvitnisson; he runs in front of her and wants to catch the moon — and that is what will happen.

## The Reveal, Seat by Seat

### Space, Astronomy & Celestial Science

*The moon-chaser — the wolf who runs before the bright bride of heaven and takes her at the end.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

### Pet Care & Animal Industries

*Hróðvitnir's son — the pursuing wolf of the Ironwood brood.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

### Meteorology & Weather Intelligence

*The eclipse-wolf of the skalds — the darkening of the moon given legs.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

## Not the First Rebrand

Hati has no cult, no continental cognate, and no existence outside the Eddic record: he belongs to the North's own eschatological machinery.  Scholars since the nineteenth century have noted that the doubling of the apocalyptic wolf — one chasing the sun, one the moon — is probably a secondary systematization of the older single figure, the bound Fenrir who breaks loose at the world's end; Simek and Lindow treat Skǫll and Hati as elaborations within the Fenrir-complex rather than independent tradition. The office is only the latest translation.
